hints: Notice the products are called free radicals, so think about what that tells you about how the shared electrons in the bond must have split.
Remember homolytic means one electron goes to each fragment, while heterolytic means both electrons go to one fragment to make ions.
Check the atomic number of bromine on the Periodic Table and remember a free radical is neutral, so its electron count equals its proton count.
walkthrough:
**Identify the fission type from the products**

Free radicals are formed, and a radical has an unpaired electron. That can only happen if the covalent bond breaks evenly, with one electron going to each side.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3^{\bullet} + \text{Br}^{\bullet}$$

**Name that fission type**

Even splitting of the electron pair is homolytic fission. Uneven splitting to give a cation and an anion would be heterolytic fission, which does not give radicals.

**Count electrons in a bromine radical**

Bromine has atomic number 35, so a bromine atom has 35 protons and 35 electrons. A bromine free radical, $\text{Br}^{\bullet}$, is still a neutral atom, it has just gained its one electron from the broken bond, so it still has 35 electrons in total.

options.A: Correct. Formation of two radicals proves homolytic fission, and neutral bromine (Z = 35) has 35 electrons.
options.B: Incorrect. Heterolytic fission gives ions ($\text{CH}_3^+$ and $\text{Br}^-$), not radicals. Students who pick this may confuse any bond breaking with heterolysis.
options.C: Incorrect. Homolytic is right, but 36 is wrong. 36 electrons would be the bromide ion, $\text{Br}^-$, which has gained an extra electron. A radical is neutral with 35 electrons.
options.D: Incorrect on both counts. Heterolytic gives ions not radicals, and 36 electrons is the $\text{Br}^-$ ion count, not the neutral $\text{Br}^{\bullet}$ radical count.
